samples.text:
In many countries today, more and more old people feel lonely. Their children often live far away and many of their friends have already died. This essay will discuss the problems which loneliness causes and what can be done to solve it.

Firstly, loneliness is very bad for old people's health. When they have nobody to talk with, they can become sad and depressed, and some of them lose interest in life. Loneliness can also make physical problems worse, for example heart disease or high blood pressure. Secondly, lonely elderly people are more at risk if something happen to them. For instance, if an old man falls down at home and lives alone, maybe no one will find him for a long time. Also, because they are lonely, some of them visit the doctor more often just to talk to someone, and this put pressure on the health system.

There are several things that can be done. The first solution is that families should spend more time with their elderly parents and grandparents. Even if they live far away, they can call them regularly or use video calls. Moreover, local government can organise community centres where old people can meet each other, play games and join activities like dancing or painting. Another good idea is volunteer programmes, in which young people visit elderly people at their home and help them with shopping or technology. This is good for both of them.

In conclusion, loneliness among old people cause mental and physical health problems and put them in danger. I think families, the government and volunteers should all work together to make elderly people feel more connected to the society.
samples.why: Problems and solutions both addressed · ideas relevant but not fully extended · mechanical sequencing (Firstly, Secondly, Also) · adequate vocabulary · several agreement and article errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
As populations age and family structures change, loneliness has become a growing concern among older people in many societies. This essay will consider the problems that social isolation creates and suggest some ways of tackling it.

The most serious effects of loneliness are on health. Older people who have little contact with others are more likely to suffer from depression and a sense that they are no longer valued, and long-term isolation is also thought to be linked to physical conditions such as heart disease and a faster decline in memory. Loneliness can also create practical dangers. An elderly person living alone who falls or becomes suddenly ill may not receive help for many hours. Moreover, these problems have a wider cost for society, as isolated older people tend to rely more heavily on health and care services, sometimes visiting their doctor partly for the social contact.

Addressing loneliness requires efforts from families, communities and governments. Families are clearly the first source of support, and even when relatives live far away, regular phone or video calls can make a significant difference. However, not every older person has close family, so community initiatives are equally important. Local councils could fund day centres, clubs and classes that give older residents a reason to leave the house and meet others with similar interests. Befriending schemes, in which volunteers make regular visits or phone calls, has also proved valuable. Another promising idea is intergenerational projects, such as bringing schoolchildren to care homes, which benefit both age groups.

In conclusion, loneliness among the elderly damages their mental and physical wellbeing and increases the demand on public services. A combination of family involvement, community activities and volunteer schemes would help older people to remain connected and active members of society.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · health, safety and social costs extended and supported · solutions logically sequenced from family to community · good range of vocabulary (befriending schemes, intergenerational) · one agreement slip.

samples.text:
In many societies, a combination of longer life expectancy, smaller families and greater geographical mobility has left a growing number of older people living alone with limited social contact. The resulting loneliness is far more than a private sorrow; it has serious consequences for health and public services, and it demands a response from families, communities and the state.

The most profound impact is on wellbeing. Prolonged isolation is strongly associated with depression and a loss of purpose, and it is increasingly recognised as a risk to physical health in its own right. Older people without regular social interaction may also experience faster cognitive decline, as conversation and shared activity help to keep the mind engaged. Isolation creates practical vulnerabilities as well: someone who lives alone and has few visitors may lie undiscovered for hours after a fall, and may be more susceptible to fraud or neglect. These individual harms translate into collective costs, since lonely older people tend to make greater use of doctors, hospitals and residential care.

Addressing the problem means rebuilding the social connections that modern life has eroded. Families remain central, and even regular calls can provide reassurance and a sense of being valued. Yet many older people have no close relatives nearby, so community provision is essential. Local authorities and charities can sustain lunch clubs, exercise groups and learning opportunities that give people both a reason and a means to leave home, provided that accessible transport is available. Volunteer befriending services offer companionship to those who are housebound, while intergenerational schemes, such as pairing students with older residents, foster mutual understanding and benefit both parties. Doctors, too, can refer isolated patients to such activities rather than relying solely on medication.

In conclusion, loneliness in later life undermines health and places growing pressure on services. Sustained investment in community networks, supported by families and volunteers, offers the most effective remedy.
samples.why: Fully addresses problems and solutions with well-extended, relevant ideas · coherent progression from individual to collective effects · precise vocabulary (cognitive decline, susceptible, housebound) · wide range of structures used accurately.
